news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh's plan shows a £14.3m gap for 2027/28, rising to £93.0m cumulatively by 2030/31
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council's medium-term financial plan forecasts a budget shortfall of £14.3m in 2027/28. The cumulative funding gap, excluding the Edinburgh Integration Joint Board (EIJB), which runs health and social care, rises to £47.3m in 2028/29, £70.8m in 2029/30 and £93.0m by 2030/31. The council's update to the plan, set out in February 2026, is in the papers for its meeting on 29 October.

A budget strategy progress update restates the 2027/28 gap from the June 2026 update. It says projections for later years are unchanged pending the Scottish Budget. The gap includes additional sums set aside for contract and other non-pay inflation, and the paper says there remains a risk around the adequacy of that provision. The council's external auditor says the council has developed medium and longer-term financial plans and that the plan shows it is financially sustainable in the short term. Its Exhibit 7 states: "There remain significant risks around long-term borrowing and funding gaps".

The council's share of the EIJB's projected gaps is shown separately: £19.7m in 2027/28, rising to £91.4m in 2030/31. Combined with the council's own gap, the total reaches £184.4m in 2030/31. The council's baseline planning assumption is that "the EIJB will address its own budget gaps without additional" council funding. It does not consider the EIJB's future pressures when developing savings plans, but says it will monitor any risk of overspend that could require additional council funding.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 7.4 - The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report - Appendix 1

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh: £4m empty-home premium for housing would raise 2027/28 funding gap from £14.3m to £18.3m
news_drafts.lead:
Dedicating £4m of new council tax income from second and long-term empty homes to housing projects would raise the City of Edinburgh Council's funding gap for 2027/28 from £14.3m to £18.3m. That is according to a report to its Policy and Sustainability Committee, which met on 20 October 2026. The gap is the further savings the council has still to find for that year, which the report calls its "incremental funding gap".

The money comes from the premium, an extra charge added to council tax on those homes. The report says the council had already assumed the new premium income when it set its 2026/27 budget, and estimates it at £4m in 2027/28. Dedicating it to new housing spending means it is not available to close the gap, which widens by the full £4m.

The report's wording is that "introducing new commitments in the way suggested in the motion would add up to £4m to the Council's incremental funding gap in 2027/28". The paper is headed "Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income".
news_drafts.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh forecasts £8.615m council-wide overspend at month three; levy-funded culture projects face December review
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council is projecting an overspend of £8.615m across all its services for 2026/27, according to the month-three budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) before the Culture and Communities Committee on 8 October. The figure was first reported to the Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September, and the paper says "an overall overspend of £8.615m is projected".

Within the committee's own area, Parks and Greenspaces is forecasting spending of £0.203m more than its £7.706m budget. The paper attributes this to "additional transport charges and the cost of temporary toilet facilities". Both are running costs rather than a rise in demand or a fall in income.

A separate paper on the Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund sets out how that money will be managed. The council will carry out an income review in December 2026, comparing the levy revenue actually collected with projections. If income is lower, the paper says, "a review will be undertaken of the remaining planned expenditure of the financial year to determine whether there is the requirement to pause projects or reduce the financial allocation". In the meantime, projects in the first year are being programmed quarterly ahead of that review.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position

findings.headline: Third-party spend fell 2.72% to £1,062,106,628 in 2025/26, with capital spend down £38.7m to £283.9m
findings.detail: The paper reports total expenditure with third parties, the fall on the previous year, and the split between capital and revenue. Revenue spend is given as about £776m, or 73% of the total.
findings.matters: A finance director tracking capital delivery can see that third-party capital spend fell by a larger proportion than total spend.
findings.figures: £1,062,106,628 total third-party spend; 2.72% reduction; £29,738,355 reduction; £283.9m capital spend; £38.7m capital reduction; approximately £776m revenue (73%)
findings.quote: Capital spend was £283.9m a reduction of £38.7m.

findings.headline: Paper names increasing service demand in Homelessness and Adult Care Services as a risk to the 2027/28 position
findings.detail: The paper lists increasing service demand, particularly in Homelessness and Adult Care Services, among the known and emerging risks to the estimated 2027/28 gap. It also cites further inflationary pressure from global uncertainty.
findings.matters: Demand-led homelessness and adult care spending is a pressure that other councils and lenders see in their own budgets, and here it is named as a risk to the gap.
findings.quote: These include increasing service demand, particularly within Homelessness and Adult Care Services, and any further inflationary pressures arising from current global uncertainty.

findings.headline: Estimated budget gap of £14.3m for 2027/28, rising to £93.0m by 2030/31, before any equivalent Edinburgh Integration Joint Board savings requirement
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 gap depends on full delivery of savings and additional income already in the approved 2026/27 budget, and on managing service demand and inflation. It assumes flat-cash core grant and a 5% Council Tax rise.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare the size of the projected gap and its stated assumptions, including flat-cash grant and a 5% Council Tax rise, against their own position.
findings.figures: £14.3m gap for 2027/28; £93.0m gap by 2030/31; 5% Council Tax rise assumed
findings.quote: indicates an estimated budget gap for 2027/28 of £14.3m, increasing to £93.0m by 2030/31, not including equivalent savings requirements for the Edinburgh Integration Joint Board (EIJB).

findings.headline: Most reported procurement savings are non-cash, and the paper describes cash savings as "challenging"
findings.detail: The paper says most savings identified are non-cash procurement savings such as cost avoidance or outcomes below market rate. It also says rebate offers depend on volume purchased. It states that cash savings continue to be challenging.
findings.matters: Savings that are cost avoidance do not reduce the cash budget, so a council closing a gap with them has to check how much reaches the revenue line.
findings.quote: The majority of savings identified are non-cash procurement savings such as cost avoidance or outcomes lower than market rate

findings.headline: Council commercial savings delivered £23.7m in 2025/26 against a £12.5m forecast, with £17.1m forecast for 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper reports that savings from existing and new commercial projects exceeded the forecast by a wide margin and rose from the previous year's £11.2m. It attributes £8.75m to Scottish Government Frameworks and £6.27m to computer hardware and electricity.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing forecast with delivered procurement savings can see the size of the beat and how much of it depends on frameworks and volume-linked rebates.
findings.figures: £23.7m delivered vs £12.5m forecast (2025/26); £11.2m previous year; £8.75m Scottish Government Frameworks; £6.27m computer hardware and electricity; £17.1m forecast for 2026/27
findings.quote: the delivered savings through existing and new commercial projects achieved £23.7m against a forecast of £12.5m, this represents an increase on the previous achievement of £11.2m
